title: The Musicians
lines: Once upon a time there was a man who had a donkey.
The donkey was old, and since he was of little use because of his age,
his master begrudged him even the thistles, and kept thinking how to get rid of him.
Though a donkey is a donkey,
he saw what his master meant to do and thought: I will run off before I am clubbed.
For oh, people are ungrateful, they are capable even of that!
Well, he did not think about it for long,
he said goodbye to the gatepost and set off. And where did he set off to?
Why, he set off straight for Brasso.
Well, why there?
Why?
Believe it or not, he had made up his mind to become a musician there.
He knew about that too, of course he did!
On and on went the donkey, and on the way he met a hound.
This hound was old too; he lay by the roadside sighing to himself:
oh, how old I have grown, oh, how weak I have become!
In the old days, when I could run well, what a good life I had!
The donkey stopped and asked:
"Why are you sighing, why are you grieving, my friend the hound?"
"How could I not sigh, how could I not grieve, when I am old and cannot run!
My master has already passed sentence on me: he will shoot me, for I am no use to him."
"Well now, if your master wants to shoot you, come with me.
I am going to Brasso to become a musician there; you can become one too.
You have a good voice, and surely you know how to play the drum as well,
you will see what a grand life you will have.
I will blow the trumpet, you will beat the drum: what fine music that will be!"
"There is sense in what you say, you have a clever tongue,"
said the hound, and he joined the donkey: off he went with him to Brasso.
They had not gone even half an hour when they met an old cat.
The poor thing was staggering by the roadside, as gloomy as three days of rain.
"And what is wrong with you, old whisker knight?"
asked the donkey.
"Oh, do not even ask," answered the cat.
"I have grown old, my teeth have fallen out,
I cannot catch mice, and my mistress wants to drown me.
Is this what I deserve?
Oh, how she petted me when I caught mice by the hundred!"
"Never you mind," said the donkey.
"Come along with us, come to Brasso to be a musician.
You know all about night music anyway,
you will have a life there like you have never had in all your days."
The cat did not think for a single minute; he shook hands with the donkey,
joined them, and now the three of them went on toward Brasso.
On and on they went, further and further,
then they came to a village, and there all at once they saw an old rooster
huddled sadly on top of a gate.
His head hung down, his wings drooped: anyone who saw him felt sorry for him.
"Good day to you, knight of the spurs!
And what is wrong with you?
My, how low you have fallen!"
"How could I not, my dear brother donkey,
when my mistress expects guests tomorrow and wants to feed them my old flesh."
"Oh, you silly thing," said the donkey, "surely you will not let them kill you.
Come with us to Brasso, join our band.
You have a lovely voice: you are just the one we were missing!"
Hop! The rooster fluttered down from the gate,
crowed a great crow, and marched off proudly with the band.
On and on they went, and by evening they came to a forest.
There they made camp at once: the donkey and the hound lay down under a big tree,
the cat and the rooster went up the tree, right to the top of it.
But before they fell asleep,
the rooster looked around, and not far away he caught sight of a firelight.
At once he called to his friends:
"Listen, I see a firelight not far from here, there must be a house there."
Said the donkey:
"Well then, let us get up and go there, for this is no comfortable place to sleep."
They did not think for long; they got themselves together and went toward the light.
As they went, the firelight grew bigger
and bigger, and all at once they were standing in front of the house.
It was a robbers' house!
The donkey, as the biggest of the band, went straight to the window and looked in.
"Well, what do you see, old donkey?"
asked the rooster.
"Oh my, oh my! A table all laid, with food and drink on it, and so much of it!
Around the table sit robbers, eating, drinking, having a merry time."
"How good it would be if we could sit down at the table too," said the rooster.
"I believe you," agreed the donkey.
All of them put their heads together and talked it over,
how they could chase the robbers away.
And since they were all very clever, the talking did not last long.
Just listen to what they did.
The donkey put his two front hooves up on the window ledge,
the dog jumped up onto the donkey's back,
the cat onto the dog, and the rooster onto the very top of the cat's head.
When they were nicely settled like this, all at once they began to make music:
the donkey brayed, the dog barked,
the cat meowed, the rooster crowed,
and to this merry music they broke the window, and whoosh, into the house!
Oh, Holy Mary, Saint Joseph! How frightened the robbers were!
They thought ghosts were about,
so up they jumped from the table and ran head over heels out into the forest.
That was just what the musicians wanted; they sat down at the table, ate, drank,
played music, and grew so merry that they nearly kicked out the side of the house.
Toward midnight they grew sleepy, put out the fire and lay down.
The donkey went out into the farmyard and lay down at the foot of a haystack,
the hound stretched out behind the door,
the cat lay down on the hearth, and the rooster flew up onto the perch.
In a minute or two they were sleeping like logs, but the robbers were not sleeping:
from far off they watched in great fright to see what was happening in their house.
Then all at once they saw the firelight go out,
and the house went dark, and they thought: perhaps the ghosts have gone.
"Go and look," said the leader to one of them, "and let us see if they have gone."
The robber went off, groped his way into the room, and went straight to the hearth,
because he saw embers glowing there.
Ah, but it was the cat's eyes.
The robber did not know that, how could he have known?
He held a match to the cat's eyes.
Well, he could hold it there, the match did not light, but something else happened!
The cat leapt at the robber's face, hissed at him and scratched him all over.
Oh, how frightened the robber was! He ran off out of his wits,
but as he ran out through the door, the dog bit him in the leg,
and as he ran across the yard howling terribly,
the donkey by the haystack gave him a mighty kick in the side.
Only the rooster did not hurt him: he woke at the noise and shouted with all his might:
cock-a-doodle-doo, cock-a-doodle-dee! and he flapped his wings.
The robber ran on out of his wits and could hardly tell what had happened to him.
"Oh, oh, let us run as far as our eyes can see, we cannot stay here.
On the hearth sits an old witch.
When I tried to light a fire, she blew in my eyes and scratched my face all over;
by the door stood a man, and he stabbed me in the leg with a big knife;
I ran into the yard, past the haystack,
and there some black monster struck me in the side with a club,
so hard that I will be a beggar from it all my life.
On the roof of the house sits the judge, and he kept shouting:
bring the robber here, bring him here!"
Well, the robbers never dared even to look toward the house again; they ran
as if they had vanished from sight,
and the musicians stayed on in the house and lived merrily for as long as they had food.
And they are living still, if they have not died.
